To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the dexterous manipulation of an object is guided by visual and tactile information, and that the neural systems associated for this guidance are distributed in the occipital, frontal, parietal, cingulate, and cerebellar cortices and cerebellum.

1) the dexterous manipulation of an object is performed with equal success using visual and tactile guidance; 2) the neural system that guides the dexterous tasks dynamically adjusts to the availability and reliability of sensory information; 3) the neural system is composed of a distributed network of regions involved in motor guidance and control, and sensory integration and processing.

(1) The neural systems that guide dexterous manipulation are distributed and integrated, and include the occipital and parietal lobes, the precentral gyrus, the cingulate gyr, the medial frontal gyrus and the cerebellum; (2) The neural systems are modulated by varying levels of visual and tactile information, but not by varying levels of task difficulty.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of motor guidance and the neural systems that acquire and process visual and tactile information.
the neural basis of dexterous manipulation.
the role of vision and touch in the control of dexterous manipulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the brain regions involved in the guidance of dexterous manipulation tasks, as revealed by fMRI, are the middle and inferior visual areas, inferior parietal cortex, primary motor cortex, and the cingulate gyruses, and that these regions are not significantly modulated by variations in visual and tactile inputs during the performance of a constant dexterous manipulation skill.
the neural systems associated for guidance of a dexterous task are modulated by varying visual and somatosensory inputs and are distributed and integrated across the brain.

a fine-tune motor task guided by visual and tactile inputs engages an integrated neural complex that consists of control and executive function regions and regions that process visual and somatosensory information.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the neural systems involved in motor guidance of a dexterous task are modulated by visual and tactile information, and the neural systems are distributed and functionally integrated to achieve the task.
the human brain is a complex system of distributed neural regions that are functionally integrated to perform a task, in this case a dexterous task, with varying levels of visual and tactile input.

a fine-tined motor task guided by various combinations of visual, tactile information engages a complex network of regions in the brain, including the occipital, parietal, and frontal lobes, the cerebellum, and the basal ganglia, that process sensory information and control and execute the motor task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human brain is able to dynamically adjust the neural systems that guide dexterous manipulation tasks to the availability and the quality of visual and tactile sensory inputs.
the human brain is capable of dynamically switching between visual and tactile guidance of dexterous tasks.
a fine-tuning of the motor task guided by the varying visual and tactile inputs engages a distributed and an integrated neural complex consisting control and executive functions.
